newsitem.title: USA: Angolan armor joins Zairean rebel drive - report.
newsitem.headline: Angolan armor joins Zairean rebel drive - report.

text.p: Troops from Angola equipped with armored vehicles and heavy artillery have joined Zairean rebel forces pushing toward Kinshasa, the Washington Post reported on Friday.

Quoting unidentified U.S. officials and reports from the region, the newspaper said the accelerating rebel advance had led to a widely shared assessment that President Mobutu Sese Seko's fall from power was imminent.
As a result, the focus of diplomatic efforts was now on minimizing the bloodshed when the forces of rebel leader Laurent Kabila entered Kinshasa, the Zairean capital, the report said.

"At this stage, the objective would be to arrange a cessation of hostilities, Mobutu stepping down and some kind of arrangement that would lead to elections," White House National Security Adviser Samuel Berger said at a meeting of Washington Post editors and reporters.
"I don't know if that's feasible or not," he added.

The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, Bill Richardson, was in Luanda, Angola, on Thursday trying to arrange a meeting between Mobutu and Kabila that would lead to an orderly transfer of power in Zaire.
With troops in Zaire and a stake in the outcome, Angola had become a key player whose restraint would be required if bloodshed were to be minimized, U.S. officials told the Post.

Several thousand former Zairean paramilitary policemen and their sons from the province of Shaba, formerly Katanga, who have been living in Angola for many years, were advancing through south-central Zaire toward the capital, the newspaper reported.

These forces wore Angolan army uniforms and had Angolan equipment, including armored personnel carriers and long-range cannons, the Post said. Regular Angolan troops also had massed in the Angolan enclave of Cabinda, north of Zaire's narrow western neck, but U.S. officials could not confirm reports that they had crossed into Zaire.
